title: The Small Weather
premise: After her mother's funeral, August Brightwater inherits a house full of unlabeled photographs and a silence she has spent three years circling: the truth about her father, the man in the pictures, who wronged a family no one in town will name. When Maren Osei, the last fluent speaker of a dying trade-language, asks August to become her final student, the lessons become an excavation — the language itself carries the story of what August's father did, and of the community that survived him. As Maren's health fails, August must choose between protecting her mother's posthumous reputation and giving the record its full, damning truth. She ends by transcribing the last sessions in full, forgiving the stranger in the photographs without excusing him, and speaking the language's final new sentence aloud at his grave.
about_author: Hazel Halloran is a former court transcriptionist who grew up in a coastal mill town and now writes about inheritance, silence, and the small weathers of ordinary injustice. She lives with her partner and an archive of other people's letters.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Silence
chapters.summary: August, first-person POV, catalogs her mother's house after the funeral: unlabeled photographs, a locked desk drawer, a man's coat that fits no one she remembers. Her aunt deflects every question. The emotional beat is grief braided with the suspicion that mourning is a form of complicity.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Speaks Alone
chapters.summary: August meets Maren Osei at the community hall, where Maren practices a dying trade-language with no one to hear it. Maren recognizes August's surname and goes quiet in a way August has learned to read. POV August. Emotional beat: the first crack of curiosity that feels like danger.

chapters.title: First Lessons
chapters.summary: Maren agrees to teach August, on one condition: the lessons happen in the old cannery, not August's house. The language has no word for 'forgive' but twelve for 'witness.' POV August. Emotional beat: the intoxication of learning something that requires her to be changed by it.

chapters.title: The Man in the Third Photograph
chapters.summary: A neighbor finally names the man in the photos: August's father, a foreman whose 'accidents' broke strikers' hands in 1989. Her mother knew and married him anyway. POV August with an interleaved second-person address to her dead mother. Emotional beat: the vertigo of inherited guilt.

chapters.title: Twelve Words for Witness
chapters.summary: Maren begins teaching the language's testimony-forms, revealing she was a striker's daughter and that the language survived precisely because workers hid it from foremen like August's father. POV August. Emotional beat: the student realizing the classroom was chosen as a courtroom.

chapters.title: What the Mother Kept
chapters.summary: August unlocks the desk drawer: her mother's unsent letters to Maren, decades of attempted apology, and evidence her mother testified — then recanted — at the inquest. POV August. Emotional beat: fury at the dead, and the terrifying discovery that silence was a decision made daily.

chapters.title: The Lesson That Stops
chapters.summary: Maren suffers a stroke mid-lesson; in the ambulance she grips August's wrist and speaks a full sentence August cannot yet translate. The town closes ranks, urging August to let the past stay buried. POV August. Emotional beat: time collapsing — the deadline becomes literal.

chapters.title: Rising Weather
chapters.summary: Working from Maren's notebooks, August deciphers the sentence: it names the second man involved, a respected town founder still alive. Confronting him, she is offered money and a version of history with her mother erased from blame. POV August. Emotional beat: the corrupting sweetness of being offered power over the story.

chapters.title: The Last Session
chapters.summary: Climax. August brings the founder's confession — recorded — to Maren's hospice bed and asks her to translate it into the language for the archive. Maren does, then asks August the question she has avoided all book long: whether she will forgive her father. POV August. Emotional beat: the choice made in a whisper.

chapters.title: One New Sentence
chapters.summary: Maren dies; the archive is donated with the founder's name intact. August, now the language's only remaining speaker, stands at her father's unmarked grave and speaks a new sentence — the language's first word for forgiveness, which she and Maren coined together. POV August. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into custody of the truth.
